Slides accessible here: `pengyunc.github.io/TSAF_Week6` ## This tutorial In this tutorial, we demonstrate forecasting the 2020Q1 CPI level, including stationarity tests, ARIMA model selection, and the final forecast computation.
:::{.callout-note title = "Agenda"} - Exercise 1(a): Transform CPI levels into log differences and select the ADF specification (lags). - Exercise 1(b): Test the log-differenced series for a unit root (ADF). - Exercise 1(c): Select the ARIMA model using AICc and Ljung–Box diagnostics. - Exercise 1(d): Forecast 2020Q1 inflation and the CPI level. - Exercise 2: Explain why first differencing removes a linear trend. :::
## We know that taking the logs is not enough... {auto-animate="true"} Recall the unit root test results for log `CPI` from Self-directed Activities 5. ```{r} dt <- read.csv("CPI.csv") Y <- ts(log(dt$CPI), start = c(1922,2), end = c(2025,2), frequency=4) Y <- window(Y, start = c(1946,1), end = c(2019,4)) ```
```{r} plot(Y) ``` An upward trend is obvious $\to$ add a time trend in deterministic specification ## We know that taking the logs is not enough... {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Carry out an ADF test of `Y`, present (i) the estimated test equation, (ii) the $t_{\text{ADF}}$ test statistic, 5\% critical value and decision, and (iii) its $p$-value. :::
```{r} library(urca) # For use of ur.df function adf <- ur.df(Y, type = "trend", selectlags = "AIC") p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "ct", statistic = "t") ```
::: {.panel-tabset} ## (i) test equation The test equation is: $$\Delta Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+\varphi Y_{t-1}+\sum^{p-1}_{k=1}\psi_{k} \Delta Y_{t-k}+U_{t}$$ The hypotheses are: \begin{align} H_{0}:&\;\varphi=0& &\text{($Y_{t}$ has a unit root)}\\ H_{1}:&\;\varphi<0& &\text{($Y_{t}$ does not have a unit root)} \end{align} The number of lags of $\Delta Y_{t}$ (i.e., $p-1$) is selected by an information criterion (AIC), where $p$ is the order of the underlying AR model. ## (ii) test summary ```{r} summary(adf) ``` ## (iii) $p$-value ```{r} print(p_adf) ```
Since $p=0.997>0.05$, we **fail to reject** the null hypothesis $H_{0}$: there is unit root.
$\implies$ Simply removing the trend component is not enough to make $Y_{t}$ stationary. $\implies$ We need to take the first difference of log `CPI`. ::: ## Exercise 1(a) :::{.callout-question} Next create the first difference time series $\Delta Y_{t}$ and a time series plot. Decide whether a trend is required for a unit root test for $\Delta Y_{t}$. :::
```{r} DY <- diff(Y) # DY is the log difference of the CPI -> Inflation plot(DY) ``` **Observation:** There is no evidence of a linear trend in this time series. There are some extended periods (e.g. early 1950's and 1970-80's) when inflation was higher. ## Exercise 1(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Carry out the unit root test on $\Delta Y_{t}$. Conclude how many differences are required for log CPI to be stationary. :::
```{r} adf <- ur.df(DY, type = "drift", selectlags = "AIC") p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "c", statistic = "t") summary(adf) ```
The estimated ADF test equation is: $$\widehat{\Delta(\Delta Y_{t})}=0.0031-0.258\Delta Y_{t-1}-0.4253\Delta(\Delta Y_{t-1})$$ ## Exercise 1(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Carry out the unit root test on $\Delta Y_{t}$. Conclude how many differences are required for log CPI to be stationary. :::
```{r} adf <- ur.df(DY, type = "drift", selectlags = "AIC") p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "c", statistic = "t") summary(adf) ```
The $t$-statistic is $-5.1529$, and the $5\%$ critical value is $-2.87$. Since $-5.1539<-2.87$, we **reject** $H_0$: $\Delta Y_{t}$ has a unit root. ## Exercise 1(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Carry out the unit root test on $\Delta Y_{t}$. Conclude how many differences are required for log CPI to be stationary. :::
```{r eval=FALSE} adf <- ur.df(DY, type = "drift", selectlags = "AIC") p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "c", statistic = "t") summary(adf) ```
The $t$-statistic is $-5.1529$, and the $5\%$ critical value is $-2.87$. Since $-5.1539<-2.87$, we **reject** $H_0$: $\Delta Y_{t}$ has a unit root. ::: {.fragment}
```{r} print(p_adf) ```
Alternatively, since $p=9.82\times 10^{-6}<0.05$, we **reject $H_0$: $\Delta Y_{t}$ has a unit root**. ::: :::{.fragment}
**Conclusion:** To render log CPI stationary, it is necessary to difference the series *once*. ::: ## Exercise 1(c) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA($p,d,q$) model for $Y_{t}$. :::
:::{.callout-tip} - Since first differencing is required for log CPI to be stationary, we need $d=1$. - How to select $(p,q)$? $\to$ Conduct a grid search for $p=0,\dots,4$ and $q=0,\dots,4$ :::
:::{.callout-note title="Code Structure"} - Set up container matrices for AICc values (`AICc`) and Ljung-Box test $p$-values (`LBp`) - For each $(p,q)$ combination: - Fit the ARIMA($p,1,q$) model with `Arima()` function, and extract AICc - Extract the Ljung-Box $p$-values with `checkresiduals()` function - Choose the model with the **lowest** AICc, and verify that its Ljung-Box $H_{0}$ (no autocorrelation) is not rejected. ::: ## Exercise 1(c) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA($p,d,q$) model for $Y_{t}$. :::
:::{.callout-tip} - Since first differencing is required for log CPI to be stationary, we need $d=1$. - How to select $(p,q)$? $\to$ Conduct a grid search for $p=0,\dots,4$ and $q=0,\dots,4$ ::: ```{r} library(forecast) pmax <- 4 qmax <- 4 LBp <- matrix(nrow=pmax+1, ncol=qmax+1) rownames(LBp) <- paste0("p=", 0:pmax) colnames(LBp) <- paste0("q=", 0:qmax) AICc <- LBp for (p in 0:pmax){ for (q in 0:qmax){ eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(p,0,q)) capture.output(LBp[p+1,q+1] <- checkresiduals(eq, plot=FALSE)$p.value) AICc[p+1,q+1] <- eq$aicc } } ``` ## Exercise 1(c) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA($p,d,q$) model for $Y_{t}$. :::
Residual autocorrelation result (`=0` if $H_{0}$ maintained) ```{r} print(1*(LBp<0.05)) ```
Model to minimise AICc: ```{r} print(AICc==min(AICc)) ```
:::{.fragment} **Conclusion:** The chosen model is ARIMA($1,1,3$) for $Y_{t}$. ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
:::{.callout-tip} Note that we have selected ARMA(1,3) for $\Delta Y_{t}\equiv \Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ in Exercise 1(c). ::: :::{.fragment}
Forecast 2020Q1 inflation: $\Delta{}Y_{2020Q1}=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})$ ```{r} eq <- Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3)) ForecastInflation_2020q1 <- forecast(eq, h=1)$mean print(ForecastInflation_2020q1) ``` ::: :::{.fragment}
**The inflation forecast is based on an approximation…** Recall from Week 1 tutorial that for small $r$ values, $\log(1+r)\approx r$: \begin{align} CPI_{2019Q4}(1+\text{inflation}_{2020Q1})&=CPI_{2020Q1}\\ \log(1+\text{inflation}_{2020Q1})&=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})\\ \implies\qquad \color{blue}{\text{inflation}_{2020Q1}}&\approx\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4}) \end{align} ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
:::{.callout-tip} Note that we have selected ARMA(1,3) for $\Delta Y_{t}\equiv \Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ in Exercise 1(c). :::
**How can we forecast the 2020Q1 CPI?** We know that \begin{align} \color{blue}{\text{inflation}_{2020Q1}}&\approx\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4}) \end{align} :::{.fragment} thus we have $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times(1+\widehat{\operatorname{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$ ```{r} # Create a ts of CPI (i.e. not log CPI) CPI <- ts(dt$CPI, start=c(1922,2), end=c(2025,2), frequency=4) CPI_2019q4 <- CPI[which(time(CPI)==2019.75)] # Forecast CPI for 2020q1 ForecastCPI_2020q1 <- CPI_2019q4*(1+ForecastInflation_2020q1) print(ForecastCPI_2020q1) ``` ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**How can we forecast the 2020Q1 CPI?** First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times(1+\widehat{\operatorname{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$ ```{r echo=FALSE} print(ForecastCPI_2020q1) ```
:::{.fragment} Second approach: - Since we know that $\widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})}=\log(CPI_{2019Q4})+\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}$ - then we can just take the exponential of the logs: $$\widehat{CPI_{2020Q1}}=\exp(\widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})})=\exp(\log(CPI_{2019Q4})+\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$$ ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**How can we forecast the 2020Q1 CPI?** First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times(1+\widehat{\operatorname{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$ ```{r echo=FALSE} print(ForecastCPI_2020q1) ```
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI_{2020Q1}}=\exp(\log(CPI_{2019Q4})+\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$ ```{r} n <- length(Y) ForecastY_2020Q1 <- Y[n] + ForecastInflation_2020q1 print(ForecastY_2020Q1) # Forecasted log CPI at 2020Q1 ```
```{r} ForecastCPI_2020q1 <- exp(ForecastY_2020Q1) print(ForecastCPI_2020q1) # Forecasted CPI level at 2020Q1 ``` ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
:::{.callout-tip} Recall that we modeled $\Delta Y_{t}$ as ARMA(1,3) $\Rightarrow$ $Y_{t}$ should be modeled as ARMA(1,1,3). ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## ARIMA(1,1,3) for $Y_{t}\equiv\log(CPI_{t})$ ```{r} eq1 = Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), xreg = (1:n)) print(eq1) ```
$\displaystyle\textsf{The model is:}\quad\boxed{\quad\begin{aligned} \color{blue}{Y_{t}}\,&\color{blue}{=\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}}\\ \Delta Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}+\theta_{3}U_{t-3} \end{aligned}\quad}$ ::: {.absolute top="530px" left="820px" style="font-size: 36px;"} These are two versions of the same model and give equivalent coefficient estimates! ::: ## ARMA(1,3) for $\Delta Y_{t}\equiv\Delta \log(CPI_{t})$ ```{r} eq = Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3)) print(eq) ``` $\displaystyle\textsf{The model is:}\quad\boxed{\quad\begin{aligned} \color{blue}{\Delta Y_{t}}\,&\color{blue}{=\beta_{1}+\Delta Z_{t}}\\ \Delta Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}+\theta_{3}U_{t-3} \end{aligned}\quad}$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="530px" left="820px" style="font-size: 36px;"} These are two versions of the same model and give equivalent coefficient estimates! ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
:::{.callout-tip} Recall that we modeled $\Delta Y_{t}$ as ARMA(1,3) $\Rightarrow$ $Y_{t}$ should be modeled as ARMA(1,1,3). :::
We can forecast $Y_{2020Q1}\equiv\log(CPI_{2020Q1})$ with ARMA(1,3) of $\Delta Y_{t}$ with drift: ```{r} eq = Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3)) ForecastInflation_2020q1 <- forecast(eq, h=1)$mean n <- length(Y) ForecastY_2020Q1 <- Y[n] + ForecastInflation_2020q1 print(ForecastY_2020Q1) ``` :::{.fragment}
We can also forecast $Y_{2020Q1}$ with ARIMA(1,1,3) of $Y_{t}$ with drift and trend: ```{r} eq1 = Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), xreg = (1:n)) ForecastY_2020q1 <- forecast(eq1, xreg=(n+1))$mean print(ForecastY_2020q1) ``` ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.absolute top="548px" left="250px" style="font-size: 36px;"} $\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Using either model is fine.}\;}$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="833px" left="250px" style="font-size: 36px;"} $\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Using either model is fine.}\;}$ ::: ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** Both approaches are approximations. :::{.fragment}
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$ ::: :::{.fragment}
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\log(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}))$ ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** Both approaches are approximations.
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\color{teal}{\log(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1})}\color{black}{)}$
The inner part is an estimate of an expectation conditional on information set $\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}$: $$\widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})}\equiv\hat{Y}_{2020Q1}=\hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{2020Q1}\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]$$ :::{.fragment} $$\implies \widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})}=\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]$$ and this is estimated through the ARIMA(1,1,3) model fitted on $Y_{t}$. ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** Both approaches are approximations.
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\color{blue}{\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]}\color{black}{)}$
**Question:** Does the following hold? $$\color{blue}{\mathbb{E}[{CPI}_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\overset{?}{=}\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])}$$ :::{.fragment} **Answer:** No. This is because of Jensen's inequality - since $\exp(x)$ is convex: $$\mathbb{E}[\exp(\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4})]>\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])$$ ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** Both approaches are approximations.
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\color{black}{)}$
Thus this estimator is actually biased for the conditional mean $\mathbb{E}[CPI_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]$: $$\mathbb{E}[CPI_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]>\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])$$ :::{.fragment} Nevertheless, in practice, simply taking the exponential tends to work well in providing a good approximation. ::: ## Exercise 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} It seems like if $Y_{t}$ has a linear trend then $\Delta Y_{t}$ does not. Explain why this is. :::
:::{.callout-note} Recall from Exercise 1(d): ARIMA(1,1,3) with trend on $Y_{t}$ produced the same parameter estimates as ARMA(1,3) with drift on $\Delta Y_{t}$. Why is that? :::
:::{.fragment} The `Arima` function is estimating the following set of equations:
::: ::: {.incremental} - ARIMA(1,1,3) with drift and trend for $Y_{t}$: \begin{align*} Y_{t}&= \beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}\\ \Delta Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{t} U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}+\theta_{3}U_{t-3} \end{align*}
- ARMA(1,3) with drift for $\Delta Y_{t}$: \begin{align*} \Delta Y_{t}&= \alpha+W_{t}\\ W_{t}&=\phi_{1}W_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{t} U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}+\theta_{3}U_{t-3} \end{align*} ::: :::{.fragment} If both gives the exact same estimates, then $\alpha=\beta_{1}$ and $W_{t}=\Delta Z_{t}$. ::: ## Exercise 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} It seems like if $Y_{t}$ has a linear trend then $\Delta Y_{t}$ does not. Explain why this is. :::
:::{.callout-note} Show that $\alpha=\beta_{1}$, $W_{t}=\Delta Z_{t}$ in the following equations: $$Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}\qquad\qquad\Delta Y_{t}=\alpha+W_{t}$$ :::
:::{.fragment} Subtract $Y_{t-1}$ on both sides gives: $$Y_{t}\,\color{blue}{-\,Y_{t-1}}\color{black}{\,=(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t})}\color{blue}{\,-\,(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}(t-1)+Z_{t-1})}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} Then simplify: \begin{align*} Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}&=\beta_{0}-\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}(t-(t-1))+Z_{t}-Z_{t-1}\\ \Delta Y_{t}&=\beta_{1}+\Delta Z_{t} \end{align*} ::: :::{.fragment} We have thereby shown that $\alpha=\beta_{1}$ and $W_{t}=\Delta Z_{t}$.
::: :::{.fragment} In addition, we have shown that taking the first difference removes the linear trend. $$Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}\quad\xrightarrow{\;\textsf{take first difference}\;}\quad \Delta Y_{t}=\beta_{1}+\Delta Z_{t}$$ ::: ## {data-background-color="#000F46"}
Thank you for coming!

:::{.callout-note title="Code Structure"} - Set up container matrices for AICc values (`AICc`) and Ljung-Box test $p$-values (`LBp`) - For each $(p,q)$ combination: - Fit the ARIMA($p,1,q$) model with `Arima()` function, and extract AICc - Extract the Ljung-Box $p$-values with `checkresiduals()` function - Choose the model with the **lowest** AICc, and verify that its Ljung-Box $H_{0}$ (no autocorrelation) is not rejected. ::: ## Exercise 1(c) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA($p,d,q$) model for $Y_{t}$. :::
:::{.callout-tip} - Since first differencing is required for log CPI to be stationary, we need $d=1$. - How to select $(p,q)$? $\to$ Conduct a grid search for $p=0,\dots,4$ and $q=0,\dots,4$ ::: ```{r} library(forecast) pmax <- 4 qmax <- 4 LBp <- matrix(nrow=pmax+1, ncol=qmax+1) rownames(LBp) <- paste0("p=", 0:pmax) colnames(LBp) <- paste0("q=", 0:qmax) AICc <- LBp for (p in 0:pmax){ for (q in 0:qmax){ eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(p,0,q)) capture.output(LBp[p+1,q+1] <- checkresiduals(eq, plot=FALSE)$p.value) AICc[p+1,q+1] <- eq$aicc } } ``` ## Exercise 1(c) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA($p,d,q$) model for $Y_{t}$. :::
Residual autocorrelation result (`=0` if $H_{0}$ maintained) ```{r} print(1*(LBp<0.05)) ```
Model to minimise AICc: ```{r} print(AICc==min(AICc)) ```
:::{.fragment} **Conclusion:** The chosen model is ARIMA($1,1,3$) for $Y_{t}$. ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
:::{.callout-tip} Note that we have selected ARMA(1,3) for $\Delta Y_{t}\equiv \Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ in Exercise 1(c). ::: :::{.fragment}
Forecast 2020Q1 inflation: $\Delta{}Y_{2020Q1}=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})$ ```{r} eq <- Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3)) ForecastInflation_2020q1 <- forecast(eq, h=1)$mean print(ForecastInflation_2020q1) ``` ::: :::{.fragment}
**The inflation forecast is based on an approximation…** Recall from Week 1 tutorial that for small $r$ values, $\log(1+r)\approx r$: \begin{align} CPI_{2019Q4}(1+\text{inflation}_{2020Q1})&=CPI_{2020Q1}\\ \log(1+\text{inflation}_{2020Q1})&=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})\\ \implies\qquad \color{blue}{\text{inflation}_{2020Q1}}&\approx\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4}) \end{align} ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
:::{.callout-tip} Note that we have selected ARMA(1,3) for $\Delta Y_{t}\equiv \Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ in Exercise 1(c). :::
**How can we forecast the 2020Q1 CPI?** We know that \begin{align} \color{blue}{\text{inflation}_{2020Q1}}&\approx\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4}) \end{align} :::{.fragment} thus we have $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times(1+\widehat{\operatorname{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$ ```{r} # Create a ts of CPI (i.e. not log CPI) CPI <- ts(dt$CPI, start=c(1922,2), end=c(2025,2), frequency=4) CPI_2019q4 <- CPI[which(time(CPI)==2019.75)] # Forecast CPI for 2020q1 ForecastCPI_2020q1 <- CPI_2019q4*(1+ForecastInflation_2020q1) print(ForecastCPI_2020q1) ``` ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**How can we forecast the 2020Q1 CPI?** First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times(1+\widehat{\operatorname{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$ ```{r echo=FALSE} print(ForecastCPI_2020q1) ```
:::{.fragment} Second approach: - Since we know that $\widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})}=\log(CPI_{2019Q4})+\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}$ - then we can just take the exponential of the logs: $$\widehat{CPI_{2020Q1}}=\exp(\widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})})=\exp(\log(CPI_{2019Q4})+\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$$ ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**How can we forecast the 2020Q1 CPI?** First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times(1+\widehat{\operatorname{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$ ```{r echo=FALSE} print(ForecastCPI_2020q1) ```
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI_{2020Q1}}=\exp(\log(CPI_{2019Q4})+\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1})$ ```{r} n <- length(Y) ForecastY_2020Q1 <- Y[n] + ForecastInflation_2020q1 print(ForecastY_2020Q1) # Forecasted log CPI at 2020Q1 ```
```{r} ForecastCPI_2020q1 <- exp(ForecastY_2020Q1) print(ForecastCPI_2020q1) # Forecasted CPI level at 2020Q1 ``` ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
:::{.callout-tip} Recall that we modeled $\Delta Y_{t}$ as ARMA(1,3) $\Rightarrow$ $Y_{t}$ should be modeled as ARMA(1,1,3). ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## ARIMA(1,1,3) for $Y_{t}\equiv\log(CPI_{t})$ ```{r} eq1 = Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), xreg = (1:n)) print(eq1) ```
$\displaystyle\textsf{The model is:}\quad\boxed{\quad\begin{aligned} \color{blue}{Y_{t}}\,&\color{blue}{=\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}}\\ \Delta Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}+\theta_{3}U_{t-3} \end{aligned}\quad}$ ::: {.absolute top="530px" left="820px" style="font-size: 36px;"} These are two versions of the same model and give equivalent coefficient estimates! ::: ## ARMA(1,3) for $\Delta Y_{t}\equiv\Delta \log(CPI_{t})$ ```{r} eq = Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3)) print(eq) ``` $\displaystyle\textsf{The model is:}\quad\boxed{\quad\begin{aligned} \color{blue}{\Delta Y_{t}}\,&\color{blue}{=\beta_{1}+\Delta Z_{t}}\\ \Delta Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}+\theta_{3}U_{t-3} \end{aligned}\quad}$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="530px" left="820px" style="font-size: 36px;"} These are two versions of the same model and give equivalent coefficient estimates! ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
:::{.callout-tip} Recall that we modeled $\Delta Y_{t}$ as ARMA(1,3) $\Rightarrow$ $Y_{t}$ should be modeled as ARMA(1,1,3). :::
We can forecast $Y_{2020Q1}\equiv\log(CPI_{2020Q1})$ with ARMA(1,3) of $\Delta Y_{t}$ with drift: ```{r} eq = Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3)) ForecastInflation_2020q1 <- forecast(eq, h=1)$mean n <- length(Y) ForecastY_2020Q1 <- Y[n] + ForecastInflation_2020q1 print(ForecastY_2020Q1) ``` :::{.fragment}
We can also forecast $Y_{2020Q1}$ with ARIMA(1,1,3) of $Y_{t}$ with drift and trend: ```{r} eq1 = Arima(Y, order = c(1,1,3), xreg = (1:n)) ForecastY_2020q1 <- forecast(eq1, xreg=(n+1))$mean print(ForecastY_2020q1) ``` ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.absolute top="548px" left="250px" style="font-size: 36px;"} $\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Using either model is fine.}\;}$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="833px" left="250px" style="font-size: 36px;"} $\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Using either model is fine.}\;}$ ::: ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** Both approaches are approximations. :::{.fragment}
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$ ::: :::{.fragment}
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\log(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}))$ ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** Both approaches are approximations.
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\color{teal}{\log(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1})}\color{black}{)}$
The inner part is an estimate of an expectation conditional on information set $\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}$: $$\widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})}\equiv\hat{Y}_{2020Q1}=\hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{2020Q1}\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]$$ :::{.fragment} $$\implies \widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})}=\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]$$ and this is estimated through the ARIMA(1,1,3) model fitted on $Y_{t}$. ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** Both approaches are approximations.
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\color{blue}{\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]}\color{black}{)}$
**Question:** Does the following hold? $$\color{blue}{\mathbb{E}[{CPI}_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\overset{?}{=}\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])}$$ :::{.fragment} **Answer:** No. This is because of Jensen's inequality - since $\exp(x)$ is convex: $$\mathbb{E}[\exp(\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4})]>\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])$$ ::: ## Exercise 1(d) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020. :::
**Remarks on the CPI forecasts:** Both approaches are approximations.
First approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})$
Second approach: $\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\color{black}{)}$
Thus this estimator is actually biased for the conditional mean $\mathbb{E}[CPI_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]$: $$\mathbb{E}[CPI_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]>\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])$$ :::{.fragment} Nevertheless, in practice, simply taking the exponential tends to work well in providing a good approximation. ::: ## Exercise 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} It seems like if $Y_{t}$ has a linear trend then $\Delta Y_{t}$ does not. Explain why this is. :::
:::{.callout-note} Recall from Exercise 1(d): ARIMA(1,1,3) with trend on $Y_{t}$ produced the same parameter estimates as ARMA(1,3) with drift on $\Delta Y_{t}$. Why is that? :::
:::{.fragment} The `Arima` function is estimating the following set of equations:
::: ::: {.incremental} - ARIMA(1,1,3) with drift and trend for $Y_{t}$: \begin{align*} Y_{t}&= \beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}\\ \Delta Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}\Delta Z_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{t} U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}+\theta_{3}U_{t-3} \end{align*}
- ARMA(1,3) with drift for $\Delta Y_{t}$: \begin{align*} \Delta Y_{t}&= \alpha+W_{t}\\ W_{t}&=\phi_{1}W_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{t} U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}+\theta_{3}U_{t-3} \end{align*} ::: :::{.fragment} If both gives the exact same estimates, then $\alpha=\beta_{1}$ and $W_{t}=\Delta Z_{t}$. ::: ## Exercise 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} It seems like if $Y_{t}$ has a linear trend then $\Delta Y_{t}$ does not. Explain why this is. :::
:::{.callout-note} Show that $\alpha=\beta_{1}$, $W_{t}=\Delta Z_{t}$ in the following equations: $$Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}\qquad\qquad\Delta Y_{t}=\alpha+W_{t}$$ :::
:::{.fragment} Subtract $Y_{t-1}$ on both sides gives: $$Y_{t}\,\color{blue}{-\,Y_{t-1}}\color{black}{\,=(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t})}\color{blue}{\,-\,(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}(t-1)+Z_{t-1})}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} Then simplify: \begin{align*} Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}&=\beta_{0}-\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}(t-(t-1))+Z_{t}-Z_{t-1}\\ \Delta Y_{t}&=\beta_{1}+\Delta Z_{t} \end{align*} ::: :::{.fragment} We have thereby shown that $\alpha=\beta_{1}$ and $W_{t}=\Delta Z_{t}$.
::: :::{.fragment} In addition, we have shown that taking the first difference removes the linear trend. $$Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}\quad\xrightarrow{\;\textsf{take first difference}\;}\quad \Delta Y_{t}=\beta_{1}+\Delta Z_{t}$$ ::: ## {data-background-color="#000F46"}
